summary: This proposed standard specifies the algorithms, parameters, key formats, key sizes and signature formats for subscribers of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) who sign certificates, certificate revocation lists and other signed objects. Setting one profile helps everyone interoperate. It builds on the broader RPKI specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: A stamp used to prove who made something must follow set rules so everyone can check it. This sets the rules for the stamps used in the system that proves who owns internet address blocks.

subtitle: The one agreed set of signature and hash algorithms and key sizes that every RPKI participant uses.

tldr.problem: RPKI participants sign certificates, revocation lists and other objects, and everyone who checks those signatures has to agree on exactly which algorithms and key sizes are in use.
tldr.mechanism: The profile requires RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 signatures with SHA-256, 2048-bit RSA keys with a public exponent of 65,537, and specific object identifiers for each kind of signed product.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 6485, mainly to match what implementations already do with the CMS signature algorithm identifier. It has since been updated by RFC 8208 and RFC 8608.

today: RFC 7935 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6485. It has been updated by RFC 8208 and RFC 8608.

sections.title: Purpose of the Profile
sections.content:
This document sets four things used by Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) subscribers when they apply digital signatures: the signature algorithm and its parameters, the hash algorithm and its parameters, the public and private key formats, and the signature format.

They apply to certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) signed objects such as Route Origin Authorizations (RFC 6482) and manifests (RFC 6486), and certification requests. Relying parties use the same algorithms to verify those signatures.

Other RPKI documents that used to point to RFC 6485 now point here, including the certificate policy, the certificate profile (RFC 6487), the architecture (RFC 6480) and the signed object template (RFC 6488).
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who signs or checks these papers needs to use the same kind of pen and the same way of writing the signature, or the checks would not work.

sections.title: The Two Algorithms
sections.content:
Two cryptographic algorithms are used. The signature algorithm is RSA PKCS #1 version 1.5 (also called RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5), taken from RFC 3447. The hashing algorithm is SHA-256. The one exception is SHA-1, which CAs use when they generate authority and subject key identifiers.

In certificates, CRLs and certification requests, the hash and signature algorithms are named together as a single identifier. The object identifier sha256WithRSAEncryption from RFC 4055 MUST be used in those products.

CMS SignedData is different because it names the hash and the signature separately. The identifier for SHA-256 MUST be used for the digest algorithm fields, and the identifier for rsaEncryption MUST be used for the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field when generating objects. When verifying, implementations MUST accept either rsaEncryption or sha256WithRSAEncryption in that field, for compatibility with objects made under RFC 6485.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone uses the same lock-and-key method and the same way of squishing a document into a short fingerprint. Some signed papers write down the two choices together, others write them separately.

sections.title: Key Pairs and Signature Format
sections.content:
The RSA key pairs used to compute signatures MUST have a 2048-bit modulus and a public exponent of 65,537.

The public key goes in the subjectPublicKeyInfo structure from RFC 5280. Its algorithm field MUST carry the object identifier for RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 with SHA-256 together with the parameters value from RFC 4055, and the key itself MUST be encoded as an RSAPublicKey. The private key format is left to local policy.

A certificate's signature field follows RFC 4055, and the signature in CMS SignerInfos follows RFC 5652.
sections.plainLanguage: The key has a required size, so it is hard to guess. How you store your own secret key at home is up to you, but the public part must be written down in one agreed way.

sections.title: Security and Future Change
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security text of its own. It points to the security considerations of RFC 4055, RFC 5280 and RFC 6487 for certificates and CRLs, to those of RFC 2986, RFC 4211 and RFC 6487 for certification requests, and to those of RFC 5754 for CMS signed objects. It states that no new security threats are introduced by this specification.

The profile expects to change. Key sizes and algorithms will probably need updating over time to keep an acceptable level of cryptographic security, and this profile should be replaced when that happens. The transition procedures are specified in RFC 6916.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks get weaker as burglars get better tools, so the rules say they will be swapped for stronger ones later, using a plan written in another document.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 6485
sections.content:
The main change is technical. RFC 6485 required sha256WithRSAEncryption in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field of CMS signed objects, but existing implementations used rsaEncryption. The RFC says support for rsaEncryption in third-party libraries is better, perhaps because RFC 3370 requires it while identifiers that combine RSA and a digest are optional.

Rather than make implementations switch, this document follows existing practice. It calls this an identifier change, not a cryptographic algorithm change, since CMS has a separate digest field that already had to hold the SHA-256 identifier. Relying parties must still accept sha256WithRSAEncryption if they see it.

Other changes include wording and typo fixes, corrected references, added citations, a corrected CRMF field name, mentions of certification requests alongside the other products, and a pointer to RFC 6916 in place of the old text on algorithm agility.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule asked for a name nobody was using. Instead of making everyone change, the rule was fixed to match what people already did, and the old name is still accepted.
